claim: The metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs) form a family of neuromodulatory G-protein-coupled receptors that contain both a seven-helix transmembrane domain (TMD) and a large extracellular ligand-binding domain (LBD) which enables stable dimerization.
source: The metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs) form a family of neuromodulatory G-protein-coupled receptors that contain both a seven-helix transmembrane domain (TMD) and a large extracellular ligand-binding domain (LBD) which enables stable dimerization.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about mGluRs that draws from established scientific knowledge about their structure and function.

claim: A variable region within transmembrane helix 4 (TM4) contributes to homo- and heterodimerization in a subtype-specific manner and tunes orthosteric, allosteric, and basal activation.
source: We uncover a variable region within transmembrane helix 4 (TM4) that contributes to homo- and heterodimerization in a subtype-specific manner and tunes orthosteric, allosteric, and basal activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study including single molecule fluorescence, molecular dynamics, functional assays, and conformational sensors.

claim: A conserved inter-TM6 interface plays a critical role in stabilizing the active state during orthosteric or allosteric activation.
source: We also confirm a critical role for a conserved inter-TM6 interface in stabilizing the active state during orthosteric or allosteric activation.
evidence: This claim is confirmed through experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Inter-TMD assembly and dynamic rearrangement drive mGluR function with distinct properties between subtypes.
source: Together this study shows that inter-TMD assembly and dynamic rearrangement drive mGluR function with distinct properties between subtypes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Dimerization or higher order oligomerization can shape the ligand sensitivity or signaling dynamics of a protein complex by producing various forms of allostery and cooperativity or mediate the formation of binding, functional, or regulatory sites.
source: Dimerization or higher order oligomerization can shape the ligand sensitivity or signaling dynamics of a protein complex by producing various forms of allostery and cooperativity or mediate the formation of binding, functional, or regulatory sites (Changeux and Christopoulos, 2016; Katzung, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The proposed dimerization of family A GPCRs has sparked intense debate.
source: The proposed dimerization of family A GPCRs, such as rhodopsin or the beta-adrenergic receptors, has sparked intense debate (Ferré et al., 2014; Milligan et al., 2019; Sleno and Hébert, 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature documenting the debate.

claim: Recent studies show that dimerization of family A GPCRs is likely transient.
source: with recent studies showing that dimerization is likely transient (Hern et al., 2010; Kasai et al., 2011; Meral et al., 2018; Işbilir et al., 2020; Möller et al., 2020; Felce et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to recent studies.

claim: Dimerization is not generally required for G protein activation in family A GPCRs.
source: and is not generally required for G protein activation (Bayburt et al., 2007; Whorton et al., 2008; Whorton et al., 2007; Kuszak et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Family C GPCRs contain canonical seven-helix transmembrane domains (TMDs) but are distinguished by their large, bi-lobed, extracellular ligand binding domains (LBDs), which are essential for their constitutive homo- and heterodimerization.
source: Family C GPCRs contain canonical seven-helix transmembrane domains (TMDs) but are distinguished by their large, bi-lobed, extracellular ligand binding domains (LBDs), which are essential for their constitutive homo- and heterodimerization (Romano et al., 1996; Doumazane et al., 2011; Levitz et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Reconstituted mGluR2 monomers are unable to undergo glutamate-mediated G-protein activation.
source: Unlike family A GPCRs, reconstituted mGluR2 monomers are unable to undergo glutamate-mediated G-protein activation (El Moustaine et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: mGluR2 monomers can be activated by TMD-targeting allosteric drugs.
source: although they can be activated by TMD-targeting allosteric drugs.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: mGluR LBD dimers undergo dramatic rearrangement between conformations in response to orthosteric agonists.
source: In response to orthosteric agonists, mGluR LBD dimers undergo dramatic rearrangement between conformations which both reshape and are controlled by a complex inter-LBD dimer interface, as deciphered through crystallographic (Kunishima et al., 2000; Tsuchiya et al., 2002; Muto et al., 2007; Koehl et al., 2019) and spectroscopic (Levitz et al., 2016; Vafabakhsh et al., 2015; Olofsson et al., 2014) studies.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to crystallographic and spectroscopic studies.

claim: Glutamate and other agonists produce relative motions between the TMDs that occur on fast millisecond time scales that precede eventual receptor activation.
source: A series of Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) studies of full-length mGluR1 have shown that glutamate and other agonists produce relative motions between the TMDs that occur on fast millisecond time scales that precede eventual receptor activation (Hlavackova et al., 2012; Marcaggi et al., 2009; Grushevskyi et al., 2019; Tateyama et al., 2004; Tateyama and Kubo, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to FRET studies.

claim: TMD-targeting allosteric drugs are able to produce intersubunit rearrangements autonomously without allosteric input from the LBDs.
source: Notably, we recently developed an isolated TMD FRET sensor which showed that TMD-targeting allosteric drugs are able to produce intersubunit rearrangements autonomously without allosteric input from the LBDs (Gutzeit et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: A prior cross-linking study of full-length mGluR2 provided evidence for close proximity of TM4 and TM5 helices in inactive states and TM6 helices in active states.
source: In line with these findings, a prior cross-linking study of full-length mGluR2 provided evidence for close proximity of TM4 and TM5 helices in inactive states and TM6 helices in active states (Xue et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a cross-linking study.

claim: Crystal structures of isolated mGluR1 and mGluR5 TMDs have shown TM1-mediated dimerization or monomers, respectively.
source: Crystal structures of isolated mGluR1 (Wu et al., 2014) and mGluR5 (Doré et al., 2014; Christopher et al., 2019; Christopher et al., 2015) TMDs have shown TM1-mediated dimerization or monomers, respectively
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to crystal structure studies.

claim: A cryo-EM study of full-length mGluR5 showed no TMD interface in an inactive nanodisc-reconstituted form but a clear TM6 interface in a glutamate and positive allosteric modulator-bound pre-active state.
source: while a cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) study of full-length mGluR5 (Koehl et al., 2019) showed no TMD interface in an inactive nanodisc-reconstituted form but a clear TM6 interface in a glutamate and positive allosteric modulator-bound pre-active state.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a cryo-EM study.

claim: Cryo-EM studies of GABAB receptors showed a lipid-mediated inactive TM5 interface that re-arranged to a TM6 interface in the presence of agonist and a positive allosteric modulator.
source: Finally, a series of cryo-EM studies of the related GABAB receptors showed a lipid-mediated inactive TM5 interface that re-arranged to a TM6 interface in the presence of agonist and a positive allosteric modulator (Mao and Shen, 2020; Papasergi-Scott et al., 2020; Park et al., 2020; Shaye et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to cryo-EM studies of GABAB receptors.

claim: Recent work has revealed conformational heterogeneity between mGluR subtypes at the level of the LBDs that shape the activation properties of different homo- and heterodimers.
source: Recent work has also revealed conformational heterogeneity between mGluR subtypes at the level of the LBDs that shape the activation properties of different homo- and heterodimers (Levitz et al., 2016; Vafabakhsh et al., 2015; Habrian et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The eight mGluR subtypes are fine-tuned for their distinct roles within the synapse that require unique glutamate sensitivity, activation kinetics and other signaling properties.
source: Such findings are in line with the notion that the eight mGluR subtypes are fine-tuned for their distinct roles within the synapse that require unique glutamate sensitivity, activation kinetics and other signaling properties (Reiner and Levitz, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous review.

claim: All isolated mGluR TMDs tested show a clear propensity for dimerization.
source: Intriguingly, we recently used a single-molecule imaging approach to determine that while all isolated mGluR TMDs tested show a clear propensity for dimerization, the mGluR2 subtype shows substantially higher dimerization propensity than other subtypes (Gutzeit et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The mGluR2 subtype shows substantially higher dimerization propensity than other subtypes.
source: Intriguingly, we recently used a single-molecule imaging approach to determine that while all isolated mGluR TMDs tested show a clear propensity for dimerization, the mGluR2 subtype shows substantially higher dimerization propensity than other subtypes (Gutzeit et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: SNAP-mGluR2-TMD molecules photobleached primarily in one-step (54.1%) or two-step (41.4%) events with a small population of >3 steps (4.5%).
source: Consistent with previous work, SNAP-mGluR2-TMD molecules photobleached primarily in one-step (54.1%) or two-step (41.4%) events with a small population of >3 steps (4.5%) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: SNAP-mGluR2-TMD represents a population of 83.1 ± 1.5% dimers when normalized based on the obligatory dimerization of SNAP-mGluR2.
source: This represents a population of 83.1 ± 1.5% dimers when normalized based on the obligatory dimerization of SNAP-mGluR2 (Figure 1D; see Materials and methods) (Gutzeit et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and references a previous study.

claim: Isolated mGluR TMD constructs maintain functionality based on downstream responses to allosteric modulators.
source: Importantly, we and others have shown that isolated mGluR TMD constructs maintain functionality based on downstream responses to allosteric modulators (Goudet et al., 2004; El Moustaine et al., 2012; Koehl et al., 2019; Gutzeit et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SNAP-mGluR3-TMD molecules photobleached with a greater number of one-step (69.1%) events, less two-step (27.9%) events, and a similarly small population of >3 steps (2.9%) compared to SNAP-mGluR2-TMD.
source: Consistent with prior work, SNAP-mGluR3-TMD molecules photobleached with a greater number of one-step (69.1%) events, less two-step (27.9%) events, and a similarly small population of >3 steps (2.9%) (Figure 1C) compared to SNAP-mGluR2-TMD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: mGluR2-TMD and mGluR3-TMD show distinct dimerization propensities that are less than an obligate dimer but greater than a canonical class A GPCR, β2AR.
source: Thus, unlike their full-length counterparts which both show strict dimerization (Levitz et al., 2016), mGluR2-TMD and mGluR3-TMD show distinct dimerization propensities that are less than an obligate dimer but greater than a canonical class A GPCR, β2AR, which we used as a monomeric or minimal dimerization control (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and a citation to a previous study.

claim: SNAP-mGluR2-TMD showed greater donor recovery than SNAP-mGluR3-TMD in acceptor photobleaching experiments.
source: The percent change in donor fluorescence was greater for SNAP-mGluR2-TMD compared to SNAP-mGluR3-TMD, consistent with the interpretation that mGluR2 has a greater inter-TMD dimerization propensity compared to mGluR3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations reveal a higher dimerization propensity for mGluR2-TMD compared to mGluR3-TMD (~40% and ~25% dimeric fractions, respectively).
source: The results reveal the exploration of multiple dimeric configurations (or macrostates) for both mGluR2 and mGluR3 (Figure 1—source data 1) and confirm a higher dimerization propensity for mGluR2-TMD compared to mGluR3-TMD (~40% and ~25% dimeric fractions, respectively)
evidence: This claim is supported by computational data from coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: TM1, TM4, and TM5 are the most contributing helices in mGluR2 dimerization.
source: This analysis draws attention to TM1, TM4, and TM5 as the most contributing helices (macrostates with probabilities larger than 10%) in the case of mGluR2
evidence: This claim is inferred from the MSM analysis of coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: TM3 and TM7 are the most contributing helices in mGluR3 dimerization.
source: or TM3 and TM7 in the case of mGluR3 (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the MSM analysis of coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: Mutation of the intersubunit disulfide bridge in mGluR2 (C121A) had a minimal effect on mGluR2 dimerization.
source: Consistent with previous work (Levitz et al., 2016), mutation of this intersubunit disulfide bridge in mGluR2 (C121A) had a minimal effect on mGluR2 dimerization (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and a citation to a previous study.

claim: The equivalent mutation in mGluR3, C127A, produced a substantial twofold reduction in dimerization.
source: However, in stark contrast, the equivalent mutation in mGluR3, C127A, produced a substantial twofold reduction in dimerization (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: mGluR2-C121A-mGluR3TMD showed reduced dimerization compared to mGluR2-C121A.
source: Indeed, this construct showed normal expression (Figure 1G), but reduced dimerization compared to mGluR2-C121A (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and 1G.

claim: mGluR3-C127A-mGluR2TMD showed increased dimerization compared to SNAP-mGluR3-C127A.
source: As hypothesized, 'mGluR3-C127A-mGluR2TMD' showed unaltered expression (Figure 1G) but increased dimerization compared to SNAP-mGluR3-C127A (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and 1G.

claim: The TMD contributes to differences in dimerization between full-length mGluR2 and mGluR3.
source: Together these results indicate that the TMD contributes to differences in dimerization between full-length mGluR2 and mGluR3.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on TMD chimeras.

claim: Across all eight rat mGluRs, most TM helices show <50% sequence conservation and <30% sequence identity, while TM6 stands out as the most similar, with 96% conservation and 72% identity.
source: Across all eight rat mGluRs, most TM helices show <50% sequence conservation and <30% sequence identity, while TM6 stands out as the most similar, with 96% conservation and 72% identity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Between the group II mGluRs, conservation remains high (>70%) for all TMs except for TM4 (33%).
source: Between the group II mGluRs, conservation remains high (>70%) for all TMs except for TM4 (33%) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Outward-facing residues in TM4 exhibited the lowest (0%) sequence identity of the group II mGluR TMs.
source: Outward-facing residues in TM4 also exhibited the lowest (0%) sequence identity of the group II mGluR TMs.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis data.

claim: Differences in TM4 between the group II mGluRs have been reported to contribute to the specific interaction of mGluR2, but not mGluR3, with the 5-HT2A serotonin receptor.
source: Intriguingly, differences in TM4 between the group II mGluRs have been reported to contribute to the specific interaction of mGluR2, but not mGluR3, with the 5-HT2A serotonin receptor, a class A GPCR (González-Maeso et al., 2008; Fribourg et al., 2011; Moreno et al., 2016; Delille et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Three outward-facing alanine residues (A677, A681, A685) at the cytosolic end of TM4 of mGluR2 allow mGluR2, but not mGluR3, to interact with 5-HT2AR.
source: This interaction has been attributed to three outward-facing alanine residues (A677, A681, A685) at the cytosolic end of TM4 of mGluR2 (Figure 2A) that allow mGluR2, but not mGluR3, to interact with 5-HT2AR (Moreno et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study and reference to Figure 2A.

claim: mGluR2-TMD-3xTM4 showed a reduction in dimerization from 78.4 ± 1.4% for mGluR2-TMD to 48.4 ± 2.4%.
source: Strikingly, we found that dimerization propensity was determined by which 3xTM4 residues were present in the construct (Figure 2C). For mGluR2-TMD-3xTM4, we observed a reduction in dimerization from 78.4 ± 1.4% for mGluR2-TMD to 48.4 ± 2.4%.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: mGluR3-TMD-3xTM4 increased dimerization from 46.3 ± 1.7% for mGluR3-TMD to 70.0 ± 2.0%.
source: Conversely, mGluR3-TMD-3xTM4 increased dimerization from 46.3 ± 1.7% for mGluR3-TMD to 70.0 ± 2.0%.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: TM4 residues determine the relative dimerization propensity of group II mGluRs at the TMD level.
source: These data indicate that TM4 residues determine the relative dimerization propensity of group II mGluRs at the TMD level.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on 3xTM4 mutations.

claim: The effect of swapping the entire TMD was mimicked by only introducing the 3xTM4 mutant in full-length mGluR2-C121A.
source: Consistent with isolated TMD data, we found that the effect of swapping the entire TMD was mimicked by only introducing the 3xTM4 mutant (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: mGluR3-3xTM4 showed a 20-fold rightward shift compared to wild type mGluR3 in glutamate response.
source: Indeed, we observed a 20-fold rightward shift for mGluR3-3xTM4 compared to wild type mGluR3 (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: mGluR2-A677S, -A681F, and -A685G did not show different glutamate EC50 values compared to wild-type mGluR2.
source: Interestingly, mGluR2-A677S, -A681F, and -A685G did not show different glutamate EC50 values compared to wild-type mGluR2 (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: mGluR3-S686A, -F690A, and -G684A all exhibited significant rightward shifts compared to mGluR3.
source: Conversely, mGluR3-S686A, -F690A, and -G684A all exhibited significant rightward shifts compared to mGluR3, although no single mutant had as reduced apparent affinity as mGluR3-3xTM4 (Figure 3F; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: TM4 residues influence inter-subunit rearrangement for both mGluR2 and mGluR3 receptor subtypes.
source: Together these results confirm the importance of TM4 in group II mGluR TMD dimerization and suggest that outward-facing residues in TM4 influence inter-subunit rearrangement for both receptor subtypes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on TM4 mutations.

claim: 3xTM4 mutants produced inter-LBD FRET responses that were indistinguishable from their wild-type counterparts with identical glutamate concentration-response curves.
source: 3xTM4 mutants produced inter-LBD FRET responses that were indistinguishable from their wild-type counterparts with identical glutamate concentration-response curves (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: mGluR3 but not mGluR2 showed a clear basal FRET response to the competitive antagonist LY341495 in the absence of glutamate.
source: As previously shown, mGluR3 but not mGluR2 showed a clear basal FRET response to the competitive antagonist LY341495 in the absence of glutamate, consistent with constitutive inter-LBD dynamics that drive basal activity (Vafabakhsh et al., 2015; Levitz et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to previous studies.

claim: Glutamate application resulted in a FRET increase for both the mGluR2 and mGluR3 inter-TMD sensors.
source: Consistent with prior fluorescent protein-based constructs for mGluR1, glutamate application resulted in a FRET increase for both the mGluR2 and mGluR3 sensors (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: Glutamate responses were fully blocked by the competitive antagonist LY341495 at 5 μM.
source: As expected, glutamate responses were fully blocked by the competitive antagonist LY341495 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C,D) at the same concentration (5 μM) used for block of functional responses (Figure 4—figure supplement 3E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C-F.

claim: MNI 137 at 10 μM was only able to produce a weak, partial block of glutamate-induced FRET responses (32.0 ± 4.5% for mGluR2; 42.9 ± 7.4% for mGluR3).
source: We next asked if glutamate-induced FRET increases are blocked by TMD-targeting mGluR NAMs. We focused on the non-specific group II mGluR NAM MNI 137, which (10 μM) was only able to produce a weak, partial block of glutamate-induced FRET responses (32.0 ± 4.5% for mGluR2; 42.9 ± 7.4% for mGluR3) (Figure 4D,E; Figure 4—figure supplement 3G)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D,E and Figure 4—figure supplement 3G.

claim: A saturating concentration of the mGluR2 PAM LY48 produced weak FRET increases that were 33.5 ± 3.9% of the amplitude of the response to saturating glutamate.
source: In addition, we tested a saturating concentration of the mGluR2 PAM LY48 and, in contrast to its robust functional activation properties (Figure 3G), observed weak FRET increases that were 33.5 ± 3.9% of the amplitude of the response to saturating glutamate (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: mGluR2-3xTM4 exhibited a clear leftward-shift compared to mGluR2 in inter-TMD FRET experiments.
source: We found that mGluR2-3xTM4 exhibited a clear leftward-shift compared to mGluR2, while mGluR3-3xTM4 exhibited a rightward-shift compared to mGluR3 (Figure 4G–I)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G-I.

claim: mGluR3-3xTM4 exhibited a reduced basal FRET response to LY341495 compared to wild type mGluR3.
source: In addition, mGluR3-3xTM4 exhibited a reduced basal FRET response to LY341495 compared to wild type mGluR3 (Figure 4J,K)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4J,K.

claim: mGluR3-3xTM4 showed reduced basal activity compared to wild-type mGluR3 in GIRK channel patch clamp assay.
source: We tested basal receptor activity using the GIRK channel patch clamp assay and, indeed, observed reduced basal activity for mGluR3-3xTM4 compared to wild-type mGluR3 (Figure 4L; Figure 4—figure supplement 4B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4L and Figure 4—figure supplement 4B,C.

claim: mGluR2-3xTM4 showed a significant increase in basal activity compared to mGluR2 in patch clamp assay.
source: Using the patch clamp assay, we observed a significant increase in basal activity for mGluR2-3xTM4 compared to mGluR2 (Figure 4M; Figure 4—figure supplement 4E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4M and Figure 4—figure supplement 4E,F.

claim: TM6 is highly conserved across mGluR subtypes compared to other transmembrane helices and is 100% identical between mGluR2 and mGluR3.
source: Notably, TM6 is highly conserved across mGluR subtypes compared to other transmembrane helices and is 100% identical between mGluR2 and mGluR3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both mGluR2-TMD-I779A and mGluR2-TMD-I779W showed reduced dimerization compared to the wild type mGluR2-TMD.
source: Interestingly, both mutants showed reduced dimerization compared to the wild type mGluR2-TMD (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mutation to a nearby conserved proline (P778) in the TM6 interface also decreased TMD dimerization.
source: Mutation to a nearby conserved proline (P778) in the TM6 interface also decreased TMD dimerization (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mutation to the same conserved TM6 residue in mGluR3, I788A, produced a similar decrease in TMD dimerization.
source: and mutation to the same conserved TM6 residue in mGluR3, I788A, produced a similar decrease in TMD dimerization (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: mGluR2-I779W, -I779A, and -P778A-I779A all showed right-shifted concentration response curves compared to mGluR2 in calcium imaging experiments.
source: mGluR2-I779W, -I779A, and -P778A-I779A all showed right-shifted concentration response curves compared to mGluR2 while mGluR2-P778A was not significantly different but did show a modest left-shift (Figure 5D,F; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D,F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: mGluR3-I788A showed a 19-fold rightward shift in glutamate response compared to wild-type.
source: Similar to mGluR2, mGluR3-I788A showed a 19-fold rightward shift in glutamate response compared to wild-type (Figure 5E,F; Figure 5—figure supplement 1F)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E,F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: mGluR2-I779A showed a 12-fold rightward shift and a 29.9% reduction in maximal PAM efficacy compared to saturating glutamate in response to LY48.
source: We tested the response of mGluR2-I779A to LY48 and found a 12-fold rightward shift and a 29.9% reduction in maximal PAM efficacy compared to saturating glutamate (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: TM6 interactions play a role in allosteric activation.
source: Together, these results clearly indicate that TM6 interactions also play a role in allosteric activation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on TM6 mutations and PAM responses.

claim: mGluR2-TMD-3xTM4 showed a clear increase in dimerization following treatment with a PAM (TASP).
source: Indeed, while wild-type mGluR2-TMD showed no sensitivity to PAM or NAM treatment, mGluR2-TMD-3xTM4 showed a clear increase in dimerization following treatment with a PAM (TASP) while mGluR2-TMD-I779A showed a clear increase following treatment with a NAM (MNI 137) (Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: mGluR2-TMD-I779A showed a clear increase in dimerization following treatment with a NAM (MNI 137).
source: Indeed, while wild-type mGluR2-TMD showed no sensitivity to PAM or NAM treatment, mGluR2-TMD-3xTM4 showed a clear increase in dimerization following treatment with a PAM (TASP) while mGluR2-TMD-I779A showed a clear increase following treatment with a NAM (MNI 137) (Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Simultaneously mutating both TM4 and TM6 interfaces with 3xTM4 and I779A prevented any PAM- or NAM-induced dimerization shifts.
source: Supporting this, simultaneously mutating both interfaces with 3xTM4 and I779A prevented any PAM- or NAM-induced dimerization shifts (Figure 6A,C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A,C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: mGluR2-C121A-3xTM4 showed a clear increase in dimerization following treatment with a PAM or glutamate.
source: However, mGluR2-C121A-3xTM4 showed a clear increase in dimerization following treatment with a PAM or glutamate (Figure 6F; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: mGluR2-C121A-I779A showed increased dimerization following treatment with a NAM.
source: and mGluR2-C121A-I779A showed increased dimerization following treatment with a NAM (Figure 6F; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Addition of LY34 decreased dimerization while addition of glutamate increased dimerization for mGluR3-C127A.
source: Indeed, addition of LY34 decreased dimerization while addition of glutamate increased dimerization (Figure 6I; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6I and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: mGluR2 and mGluR3 readily form heterodimers following heterologous expression and can be co-immunoprecipitated from the frontal cortex.
source: Among the most preferred pairs are mGluR2 and mGluR3 which readily form heterodimers following heterologous expression and can be co-immunoprecipitated from the frontal cortex.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: SNAP-mGluR2-TMD was able to pull-down both CLIP-mGluR2-TMD and CLIP-mGluR3-TMD, but a higher level was observed for CLIP-mGluR2-TMD.
source: While SNAP-mGluR2-TMD was able to pull-down both constructs, a higher level was observed for CLIP-mGluR2-TMD (Figure 7B,C)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B,C.

claim: The TMD dimerization propensity of mGluR2 homodimers is higher than that of mGluR2/3 heterodimers.
source: suggesting that TMD heterodimers can form but the TMD dimerization propensity of mGluR2 homodimers is higher than that of mGluR2/3 heterodimers.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the two-color SiMPull experimental data.

claim: HA-SNAP-mGluR3-TMD showed higher levels of pulldown for CLIP-mGluR2-TMD compared to CLIP-mGluR3-TMD.
source: We performed the reverse experiment with HA-SNAP-mGluR3-TMD (Figure 7D) and found higher levels of pulldown for CLIP-mGluR2-TMD compared to CLIP-mGluR3-TMD (Figure 7E,F)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D,E,F.

claim: The inter-TMD assembly of mGluR3 homodimers has a slightly lower propensity than that of mGluR2/3 heterodimers.
source: suggesting that the inter-TMD assembly of mGluR3 homodimers has a slightly lower propensity than that of mGluR2/3 heterodimers.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the two-color SiMPull experimental data.

claim: Full-length mGluR2 preferentially assembles with mGluR3 at comparable ratios of surface-expression.
source: Consistent with previous work (Lee et al., 2020), at comparable ratios of surface-expression, full-length mGluR2 preferentially assembles with mGluR3 (Figure 7G–I; Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G-I and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A-C, and a citation to a previous study.

claim: Mutating the intersubunit disulfide-forming cysteine (C121A in mGluR2; C127A in mGluR3) resulted in a dramatic swap of the dimerization preference.
source: However, mutating the intersubunit disulfide-forming cysteine (C121A in mGluR2; C127A in mGluR3) resulted in a dramatic swap of the dimerization preference.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: HA-SNAP-mGluR2-C121A pulled down CLIP-mGluR2-C121A at nearly wild-type levels but pulled down a much lower level of CLIP-mGluR3-C127A.
source: HA-SNAP-mGluR2-C121A pulled down CLIP-mGluR2-C121A at nearly wild-type levels, consistent with the minor effect of this mutation on mGluR2 homodimerization (Figure 1F) but pulled down a much lower level of CLIP-mGluR3-C127A (Figure 7H–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7H-I and reference to Figure 1F.

claim: Introducing the 3xTM4 mutation into CLIP-mGluR3-C127A enhanced pulldown via SNAP-mGluR2-C121A.
source: To test whether inter-TM4 interactions contribute to the distinct assembly properties of mGluR2/3 heterodimers, we introduced the 3xTM4 mutation into CLIP-mGluR3-C127A and observed enhanced pulldown via SNAP-mGluR2-C121A (Figure 7H–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7H-I.

claim: This stretch of TM4 is a determinant of the assembly of mGluR2/3 heterodimers.
source: While this construct was unable to rescue mGluR2/3 heterodimerization back to the level of wild-type receptors, this result clearly indicates that this stretch of TM4 is a determinant of the assembly of mGluR2/3 heterodimers.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on 3xTM4 mutations in heterodimers.

claim: mGluR2/3 TMD dimers show an intermediate propensity compared to their parent homodimers.
source: Together these data indicate that mGluR2/3 TMD dimers show an intermediate propensity compared to their parent homodimers (Figure 7L)
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data and shown in Figure 7L.
